source.title: When Is Multilinguality a Curse? Language Modeling for 250 High- and Low-Resource Languages
source.authors: Tyler A. Chang; Catherine Arnett; Zhuo-Wen Tu; Benjamin K. Bergen

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out language-model performance across monolingual dataset sizes and validates predictions from fitted curves, but uses a different, limited-scale setup rather than reproducing the original parameter/data/compute scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The study fits monolingual performance curves and validates held-out token-count estimates; these bear on V1 and V2. Its multilingual-data experiments vary language composition and report interference effects, not a power-law fit or compute-optimal allocation, so they are not included as scaling-law rows. Model-size comparisons are reported as effects on multilinguality benefits or costs, not as a parameter-count scaling curve.
record.test_reason: The study fits monolingual curves only to build its own performance metric (estimated monolingual token count) for the multilingual experiments. The fitted form is −a·x^−b + c with x = log10 tokens, a power law in log-data rather than in tokens. Fit quality is given only as 'good fit on average'. Many fits rest on two points with parameters fixed to medians. Low-resource runs repeat data for 20 epochs. The held-out RMSE validates the authors' token-estimation tool, not extrapolation of loss to much larger runs. This is the scaling finding used as a tool, with only the tool's own accuracy reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The power-law-style fits are a tool for an interpretable metric, not a scaling-law test. The main conclusion is that moderate multilingual data from syntactically similar languages helps low-resource languages (up to about a 33% data-equivalent gain). Multilingual data consistently hurts high-resource languages, attributed to limited model capacity.
record.recipe_differences: Fits relative evaluation log-likelihood against monolingual dataset size for small GPT-2 models and validates inferred token counts; it does not reproduce joint scaling over model parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Curves vary across languages. For languages with too few data points, the authors constrain fitted parameters using median values from higher-resource languages; they also report that larger datasets improve performance primarily for larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative eval log-likelihood of tiny/mini/small GPT-2 models (4.6M–29.5M) is well fit on average across 252 languages by −a·(log10 D)^−b + c. Curves vary substantially across languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Monolingual LM log-likelihood versus log dataset size follows a saturating power law in log-tokens for small models across many languages.

fits_no_version.finding: Inverting language-specific fits to estimate held-out monolingual token counts gives RMSE of 0.340, 0.317 and 0.335 log10 tokens (tiny, mini, small).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitted dataset-size curves allow approximate inference of equivalent data size from loss in small multilingual-study models.

fits_no_version.finding: At 1M tokens, the three model sizes perform similarly; larger datasets help mainly the larger models (§4.3, Figure 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-bottlenecked regimes erase the benefit of model size in small LMs.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The tested models are small (up to 29.5M parameters for monolingual baselines), and many language-specific curves use parameter constraints because there are too few data points to fit them independently. The study evaluates token-count estimates rather than reporting direct held-out loss-prediction errors.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows omitted. Multilingual-data quantity and language-similarity outcomes in Figures 3–5 were not extracted as scaling-law results because they concern language-distribution interference rather than a fitted loss-versus-total-training-tokens law or compute-optimal allocation.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in tokens, parameters or compute. The fit form uses log10 tokens and serves as a metric.
No forecast of loss for runs orders of magnitude larger; only token-count estimation within 1M–1B tokens on small models.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or regimes tested as scaling laws.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V1/V2 supports labels are removed. The curve is in log10 tokens, many fits are constrained to median parameters with 1–2 points, and the validation measures the authors' own estimator. The models are tiny (≤45.8M parameters).

versions.untested_parts: Tests performance versus monolingual dataset size at three small model sizes. Does not test power laws in parameter count or compute, or the stated non-bottleneck regimes.
Validates held-out token-count estimates from monolingual curves at small model sizes; does not test direct forecasting of loss for much larger models or runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocation.
Does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, fine-tuning, transfer, or repeated-data scaling-law tests.
No downstream-task performance evaluation; cited downstream predictability is from other work.
Does not compare scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices or setups, or test systematic bending from a fitted scaling law.

rows.subject: GPT-2 tiny
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to monolingual evaluation relative log-likelihood versus dataset size.

conditions.value: fixed monolingual tokenizer per target language

rows.measure: Fit of −ax^-b + c to relative evaluation log-likelihood versus monolingual dataset size (x in log10 tokens).
rows.value: The authors report that −ax^-b + c provides a good fit on average across all 252 languages.
rows.note: The plotted aggregate includes lighter curves for individual languages; the text characterizes the average fit as good.
rows.check: The curve is a power law in log10 tokens, not in tokens. It is fit as a measurement tool. Fit quality is qualitative only ('good fit on average'), and data are repeated for 20 epochs at low resource. It does not measure V1's power-law loss in tokens.

rows.subject: GPT-2 tiny
rows.operation_detail: Estimate held-out monolingual token counts from curves fit to other monolingual model results.

conditions.value: held out one or more monolingual models per language; estimation extrapolates at least one order of magnitude

rows.measure: Root-mean-square error of estimated monolingual token count, in log10 tokens.
rows.baseline: Perfect token-count estimation is shown as the reference in Figure 8.
rows.note: The authors describe the held-out token-count estimates as reasonable; estimates preserve model performance rankings.
rows.check: This RMSE measures the accuracy of the study's own token-count estimator (inverse of the fitted curve), held out one order of magnitude apart, on 4.6M–29.5M models. It is the method's own performance, not loss prediction for runs orders of magnitude larger.
